top.headline: ProPublica: Five Ways Voting Could Still Be Disrupted on Election Day
top.blurb: Courts have blocked most of the administration's attempts to expand federal control over elections, but ProPublica catalogs where real risk remains today: federal agents near polling places, a dismantled CISA leaving bomb-threat and hoax response to understaffed states, aggressive DOJ monitoring, and a lawsuit seeking to block certification of an Alaska Senate race before a single vote is counted.

top.headline: After ProPublica Investigation, House Democrats Demand Answers on U.S. Citizens Detained by Immigration Agents
top.blurb: Forty House Democrats pressed DHS for numbers after ProPublica found more than 500 U.S. citizens detained by immigration agents, including 63 held while recording and roughly a dozen deported, mostly children. DHS says it does not arrest citizens and accused the lawmakers of favoring 'criminal noncitizens' over crime victims.

top.headline: GOP-Run Election Boards Cut Polling Sites at Black and Latino Colleges, Forcing Long Walks to Vote
top.blurb: Republican-majority boards in North Carolina, Texas and Ohio eliminated on-campus early voting this fall, leaving students at NC A&T, UT Arlington and Central State a 45-minute walk or longer to the nearest site. A student who organized a protest march called the result 'a modern-day poll tax'; courts have so far declined to reinstate the sites.

top.headline: Amit Shah Claims Three Crore of 13 Crore Voters Deleted in SIR Were 'Bangladeshi Infiltrators'
top.blurb: At a Hyderabad rally, the home minister broke down 13 crore voter-roll deletions as 6.2 crore relocations, nearly 3 crore deaths and over 1 crore duplicates — then said a further 3 crore 'never existed' and were Bangladeshi infiltrators Congress wanted protected. The claim lands as nationwide protests demand the Election Commission chief's resignation over the same revision.

top.headline: How a Trust Close to the BJP Got Five Elephants From Assam for Tamil Nadu Temples
top.blurb: An investigation traces how Seva Trust, run by a couple with reported ties to Amit Shah and Narendra Modi, moved five elephants from Assam to Tamil Nadu temples with ownership paperwork completed in as little as 7.5 hours and signs — ear holes, a bullet wound — consistent with wild capture. Key officials and the trust did not respond to requests for comment.

top.headline: Bombay High Court Says OCI Cardholders Can't Protest, Orders Actor Imran Khan to Apologise
top.blurb: The court extended a hold on a 'leave India' notice against the US-citizen actor after he apologised for joining an October protest against the Election Commission chief, but ruled that Overseas Citizens of India have no right to demonstrate. It warned that an Indian citizen protesting abroad would likewise be sent home; the case returns December 7.

top.headline: US Strikes Iranian Targets in Strait of Hormuz as Vance Claims 'Progress' in Talks
top.blurb: The US military carried out what officials called 'limited defensive' strikes on Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz after surface-to-air missile threats against American assets, with explosions also reported on Iran's Qeshm Island. Vice President JD Vance said indirect peace talks were making progress, but Tehran says Washington must first lift its naval blockade.

top.headline: Russian Strike Kills 26 at Ukrainian Aid Centre Zelenskyy Calls a 'Vile Terrorist' Attack
top.blurb: Two strikes hit a school-turned-shelter in Komyshuvakha, Zaporizhzhia, that served as the village's weekly aid distribution point, killing at least 26 including rescue workers and police, with dozens more feared trapped. Zelenskyy said Russia knew residents gathered there and called the timing, days before the US midterms, deliberate; US-mediated talks are now set for Abu Dhabi on November 10-11.

top.headline: Bangladesh Garment Workers Say Wages No Longer Cover Food as Protests Shut Hundreds of Factories
top.blurb: Workers earning as little as $121 a month are demanding more than double the current minimum wage, and police used tear gas on protesters in Ashulia as 529 factories supplying H&M, Zara and Walmart were disrupted. Bangladesh's wage board, formed only after the protests began, is reviewing demands as inflation has eroded real pay since the last revision in 2023.

top.headline: South Africa Beat Australia 2-1 in Test Series, Take Over World No. 1 Ranking
top.blurb: South Africa won the third Test by 176 runs to take the series 2-1, handing Australia their first Test series defeat of 2026 and knocking them off the top of the ICC Test rankings. Coach Andrew McDonald defended a struggling Marnus Labuschagne but said his place would be reassessed before Australia's home summer against New Zealand, starting in Perth on December 9.

more.headline: Glenn Maxwell Retires From International Cricket After 14-Year Career
more.blurb: The Australian all-rounder, who won two ODI World Cups and a T20 World Cup and once scored an unbeaten double-century against Afghanistan, bows out after 149 ODIs, 130 T20Is and 7 Tests.

top.headline: Self-Financed Marathi Thriller 'Gondhal' Takes an Underdog Bid at the Best International Film Oscar
top.blurb: Director Santosh Davakhar financed India's Oscar entry himself with earnings from his construction business after producers wanted changes he rejected, built it around an unknown cast and a near-24-minute opening take, and watched it underperform on release before an IFFI award revived its chances. He has since run US screenings by hand, betting festival buzz can do what marketing could not.

bengal.headline: Suvendu and BJP Turn Kolkata Rally Into Attack on Rahul Gandhi and INDIA Bloc Over SIR
bengal.blurb: Leader of the Opposition Suvendu Adhikari used a BJP rally to accuse the INDIA bloc of protecting 'infiltrators' through its opposition to the electoral roll revision, sharpening the party's line ahead of Bengal's 2026 polls.

bengal.headline: Stone Mining Scam: Retired Birbhum Land Reforms Official Arrested
bengal.blurb: Police arrested a former Birbhum land reforms officer in connection with an illegal stone mining racket, the latest arrest in a probe into how mining permissions were issued in the district.

bengal.headline: Bengal Deploys 12 IAS Officers to Speed Up CAA Citizenship Applications
bengal.blurb: The state government assigned a dozen IAS officers to process the backlog of Citizenship Amendment Act applications, days after the chief minister set a December 31 deadline for clearing them.

travel.headline: How an Irish Backroad Sport Rolled Into Small-Town America
travel.blurb: A journalist who taught himself Irish road bowling from a Library of Congress book in the 1990s built it into a 50-member West Virginia nonprofit that now ships bowling balls to players in 49 states.

travel.headline: Feared Extinct for Nearly a Century, the Bangka Slow Loris Was Never Really Gone
travel.blurb: A study of more than 90 rescued lorises shows the primate, undocumented in scientific literature since 1937, has survived all along on Indonesia's Bangka Island, though tin mining and plantations have cut its forest habitat by 62 percent since 2000.

happy.headline: A 4,000-Year-Old Dog's Paw Print, Preserved in a Bronze Age Mud Brick
happy.blurb: Archaeologists in Turkey found a dog's paw print pressed into a mud brick 4,000 years ago, a fleeting moment of ordinary life preserved by chance in the rubble of a collapsed Bronze Age house.

tech_top.headline: Anthropic Warns It May Be 'Imminently' Close to AI That Can Build More Capable AI
tech_top.pm_note: A frontier lab flagging this in a financial filing, not a safety paper, means governance and disclosure norms for AI capability jumps are about to become a live regulatory question.
tech_top.blurb: In fine print of a revised S-1 filing, Anthropic said internal estimates suggest it may soon meet its own threshold for 'dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI' — recursive self-improvement, where AI gets good enough at training itself to compound its own capabilities. The company says it has not designated any current model as crossing that line and does not expect to let Claude build its successors without human oversight.

tech_top.headline: Germany Says Lawmakers' iPhones May Have Been Hit by Spyware
tech_top.pm_note: Apple's threat notifications don't name an attacker or confirm compromise, which is exactly why they're a weak signal product and security teams should expect to keep fielding.
tech_top.blurb: Germany's federal cybersecurity office said members of the Bundestag and other prominent figures received Apple warnings of possible spyware targeting, in a campaign Apple says reached users in 99 countries. Apple does not attribute such attacks or confirm compromise, so Germany advised recipients to simply assume their devices were breached; it's unclear who is behind this round.

tech_more.headline: This Year's 'I Voted' Stickers Are Getting the AI Slop Treatment
tech_more.blurb: A writer's polling-place sticker turned out to be an AI-generated mess of garbled text and bronze laurels, a small but telling sign of how casually generative AI is creeping into civic traditions.

tech_101.text: The point at which an AI system becomes capable enough to meaningfully improve its own training process, letting its capabilities compound faster than human researchers alone could manage — the scenario AI safety researchers treat as a critical threshold to control, not race past.

Surveillance software that can infect a phone without the owner clicking a link or opening a file, often sold by private 'mercenary spyware' vendors to governments. It's why Apple's threat notifications matter even though they can't say who sent the attack.

science.headline: A Barium Catalyst Could Make Ammonia Without High Heat, Pressure or Precious Metals
science.blurb: Tokyo researchers built a cobalt-and-barium catalyst that weakens nitrogen's famously tough triple bond enough to synthesize ammonia at 300°C and modest pressure, outperforming benchmark ruthenium and industrial iron catalysts in their tests. Ammonia is mostly fertilizer today, but it's also being explored as a carbon-free way to store and move hydrogen energy.

science.headline: IceCube's 'Ghost Particles' Carry 10 Billion Times the Energy of an Ordinary Neutrino
science.blurb: The IceCube Neutrino Observatory, a cubic kilometer of instrumented Antarctic ice, catches only a few dozen of the most energetic cosmic neutrinos a year — chargeless, near-massless particles light-years of lead couldn't reliably stop. The sources of the highest-energy ones, carrying roughly ten billion times the energy of a typical solar neutrino, remain unknown.

science.headline: Jumping Spiders Twitch, Curl Their Legs and Move Their Eyes in a REM-Like Sleep State
science.blurb: University of Bonn researchers found that jumping spiders cycle between a still 'quiescence' stage and a twitchier, eye-moving stage resembling REM sleep, responding far slower to a loud noise during the latter. Spiders and vertebrates split evolutionarily some 500 million years ago, so structured sleep in both suggests the basic architecture may be very old.

philosophy.headline: Why Peacebuilding That Leaves Capitalism Intact Doesn't Actually Build Peace
philosophy.blurb: Azize Aslan argues that standard peace deals stop at ending violence and leave intact the economic relations that caused the conflict, leaving ex-combatants asking 'what now?' after the guns fall silent. She points to Rojava's bottom-up cooperatives and Colombia's ECOMÚN federation as imperfect but real attempts to build peace as a daily, collective way of living rather than a signed document.

philosophy.headline: Lamarck Said Living Things Remake Themselves and the World — Science Buried Him, Then Proved Him Partly Right
philosophy.blurb: Jean-Baptiste Lamarck, who coined the word 'biology' in 1802, argued that organisms actively shape their own bodies and environments rather than passively obeying fixed laws — a view his rival Cuvier helped bury for over a century. Jessica Riskin traces how epigenetics, niche construction and inherited behavioral adaptation are now reviving a version of his 'active life' idea that 20th-century genetics had written off.

philosophy_101.text: A distinction from peace researcher Johan Galtung: negative peace just means no active violence, while positive peace means dismantling the unjust structures — economic, political, social — that caused the conflict in the first place. Most peace deals settle for the first and call it done.

The idea that organisms don't just adapt to their environment — they actively reshape it, and that reshaped environment then changes what traits get selected for next. A coral reef or a beaver dam is as much a product of evolution as the animal that built it.
